senses: A male juvenile delinquent, originally in Jamaica in the 1960s.
A male enthusiast of ska music.
ety: Borrowed from Jamaican Creole rude bwoy, equivalent to rude + boy.
examples: Leppo had been a rudeboy since his teens, earning his first three-month jail rap for vagrancy in 1971.
Since I was a teenager I have had to play different characters, negotiating the cultural expectations of a Pakistani family, Brit-Asian rudeboy culture, and a scholarship to private school.
The rudeboy might have evolved since his ska-fuelled early days on the streets of 1960s Jamaica, but the staples are the same: nicely buffed footwear, pork-pie hats, cropped trousers and sharp suits.

senses: Father’s father; paternal grandfather.
A fungus, or some other organism closely resembling a fungus.
examples: He found the suspicion correct which supposed the tree branched from one great root, like a candelabrum; the fork, though stained and slimy with green fungoids, was quite near the ground, and offered a first foothold.

senses: Japanese women's professional wrestling
A female Japanese professional wrestler
ety: Ellipsis of 女子プロレス (joshi puroresu), itself a compound of 女子 (joshi, “woman”) + プロレス (puroresu, “professional wrestling”).
examples: Whether they are called joshis, luchadoras, or lady grapplers, one can find female wrestlers in every part of the world.

senses: Sloping (as opposed to horizontally flat or vertically upright).
examples: Her chamber is aloft, far from the ground, / And built so shelving that one cannot climb it / Without apparent hazard of his life.
We still continued winding round Skiddaw, the sides of which are every where rather shelving, than steep.
The town of Abda is built upon the top and down the steeply shelving face of an isolated rocky spur,

senses: The man stationed in the top on a sailing vessel, responsible for the setting of the sails
The uppermost sawyer in a sawpit; a topsman.
A jitterbug, originated in Harlem, New York.
ety: Probably from Lindy, the nickname of US aviator Charles A. Lindbergh.

senses: To play (a guitar or other stringed instrument) by plucking various strings simultaneously.
A nodding motion (of the head etc.).
ety: 1610s, from Latin nūtātiō (“nodding”), from nūtō (“to nod”). Compare mutation.

senses: To endow with power.
To increase the potency (of a drug or biochemical agent).
ety: From potent + -i- + -ate (verb-forming suffix), modelled after German potenzieren.
examples: These antidepressants potentiate the analgesic action of opiates.

senses: Pigmented more than normal; pigmented too much.
A small tent or shelter.
A type of bronze used for making cannons.
A dark grey or bluish-grey colour; gunmetal grey.
A Middle Eastern sandwich-like wrap of shaved lamb, goat, chicken, turkey, beef, or a mixture of these.
ety: Borrowed from Arabic شَاوِرْمَا (šāwirmā), شَاوَرْمَا (šāwarmā), from Ottoman Turkish چویرمه (çevirme, “something that is spun or turned over”), verbal noun of چویرمك (çevirmek, “to turn over”) (modern Turkish çevirme and çevirmek).

senses: The wood of beech trees (Fagus spp.).
A wood largely populated with beech trees.
That has been prepared by deionization.
Not able to be delivered.
examples: The dead letter office keeps undeliverable mail.
The ambitious project to build 500 new hospitals was later deemed to be undeliverable.

senses: A beater; a striker.
A pulsometer.
A jigging machine used in the South African diamond industry.
a Portuguese inn
examples: This pousada has several rooms that are a short hike from the main building, which is perched above the vineyards.

senses: The act of purveying.
The prerogative of the Crown to static separation of duty with goods and services for royal use.
ety: From Middle English purveiaunce et al., from Anglo-Norman purveaunce.

senses: A gardener; a person interested in or practicing horticulture.
ety: From horticulture + -ist.. By surface analysis, horti- + cult + -ure + -ist.

senses: Any device that activates or deactivates the components of a machine or system according to a preplanned sequence (as in a washing machine, or central heating system).
A device or system that orders and/or modifies digitally stored music and sound for playback.
A control device to increase/decrease the capacity of plant that is enabled to act in a specific order or sequence.
A dinner bell, (historical) a shrill little bell used to signal dinner for medieval monks.
ety: From Latin squilla, from Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla).

senses: An associate; a fellow of an academy, etc.
According to Gilles Deleuze, a social body that takes credit for production.
Sparing; stinting; parsimonious.
Miserly or stingy.
ety: From Middle English nigard, nygard (“miser”), from nig (“niggardly person”), possibly of Scandinavian origin; compare Old Icelandic hnøggr (“miserly, stingy”), Old Norse *hniggw, with descendants Swedish njugg (“stingy”), dialectal Swedish niggla (“be stingy”), dialectal Norwegian nigla. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hnauwjaz, source of Old English hneaw (“stingy”), replaced by Middle English nig. Possibly cognate to niggle (“miser”). Compare German Knicker (“niggard”), knickerig (“niggardly”). Unrelated to the word nigger, but see the usage notes.
examples: It was, however, the pleasure of his niggard and unhappy fortune, that in seeking a place proper for his accommodation, he and Dapple tumbled into a deep and very dark pit, among a number of old buildings.

senses: A charge in the form of a teardrop shape, originally with wavy sides, but now often with straight sides.
ety: From Middle English goute, from Old French goutte, goute, gote, from Latin gutta (“drop”). Doublet of gout and gutta.

senses: Certain other woody plants that resemble those of Wisteria spp..
One who, or that which, incorporates.
A cocktail consisting of half champagne and half orange juice.
ety: From New Latin mimosa, from Latin mimus (“mime, actor”), referring to Mimosa pudica and its habit of shrinking back when touched. The cocktail is named after the bright yellow, fragrant flowers of the mimosa Acacia dealbata.

senses: Any of many marine invertebrates, of the phylum Brachiopoda, that have bivalve dorsal and ventral shells with two tentacle-bearing arms that capture food
ety: Borrowed from translingual Brachiopoda. By surface analysis, brachio- + -pod.

senses: One who feasts, who attends a feast.
ety: From Middle English fester, festour, equivalent to feast + -er.
examples: All the feasters eagerly awaited the arrival of the main course.

senses: The conclusion of a passage; cadence.
The close or end of a historical period; clause.
At noontimes.
The music for a dance of this kind.
ety: From French galop; named after the fastest running gait of a horse (see gallop), a shortened version of the original term galoppade.

senses: Something or someone old.
A song or record from a previous era.
The genre of music composed of popular music from previous eras.
A light tan color inspired by the color of hazelnut.
ety: Equivalent to hazel + nut; from Middle English haselnote, from Old English hæselhnutu (“hazelnut”). Cognate with West Frisian hazzenút (“hazelnut”), Saterland Frisian Hoaselnuute (“hazelnut”), Dutch hazelnoot, German Haselnuss.

senses: A decimeter.
A silver coin of Persia, introduced by Safavid Shah Abbas in 16th century, worth about twenty cents.
A Persian unit of weight, equivalent to approximately 12.8 oz.
An Afghan bronze coin from the early 20th century, equivalent to four shahi.
A unit of measurement for Afghan postage stamps.
ety: From Classical Persian عَبَّاسِی (abbāsī); see for more. Doublet of abazi.

senses: Having glades.
Synonym of spectacular mark.
